text: Under Section 41 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh), a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant when any of the following situations exist: (a) the person is in the presence of a cognizable offence; (b) the person has been taken into custody for a cognizable offence; (c) the person is about to commit a cognizable offence; (d) the person is suspected of having committed a cognizable offence; (e) the person is a proclaimed offender; (f) the person has escaped from lawful custody; (g) the person is in breach of any condition of bail or recognizance; or (h) the person is a deserter from the armed forces. In any of these circumstances the police officer may lawfully make an arrest without first obtaining a warrant.

citations.quote: Any police officer may arrest any person without warrant who— (a) is in the presence of a cognizable offence; (b) has been taken into custody for a cognizable offence; (c) is about to commit a cognizable offence; (d) is suspected of having committed a cognizable offence; (e) is a proclaimed offender; (f) is a person who has escaped from custody; (g) is a person who is in breach of any condition of bail; (h) is a person who is in breach of any condition of recognizance; (i) is a deserter from the armed forces.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a person arrested without a warrant must be produced before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours of the arrest. If the person is not produced within that period, he must be released on bail.

citations.quote: Every person who is arrested without warrant shall be produced before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours of his arrest, and if he is not produced within that period, he shall be released on bail.

text: Under Section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a police officer may not search a woman unless the search is conducted in the presence of another woman officer, or a magistrate, or a relative of the woman. This provision ensures that a woman's privacy is protected during a search.

citations.quote: No police officer shall search a woman except in the presence of another woman officer, or a magistrate, or a relative of the woman.

text: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 does not contain provisions specifying the amount or type of physical restraint that may be used on a person who has been arrested. Such matters are governed by other statutes, police regulations, or case law, which are outside the scope of the Code.

Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a police officer must follow several mandatory steps when making an arrest. First, the officer may only arrest without a warrant if the person is caught in the act of committing an offence, is a proclaimed offender, or if the officer has reasonable grounds to believe the person has committed a cognizable offence (Section 41). Before the arrest the officer must inform the person of the grounds for the arrest (Section 41). After the person is taken into custody, the officer must record the arrest in the police diary and must produce the arrested person before the magistrate within twenty‑four hours of the arrest (Section 43). The officer must also submit a written report of the arrest to the magistrate (Section 44) and ensure that the person is kept in lawful custody, with the right to bail if applicable (Section 45). These duties together ensure that arrests are made lawfully, the arrested person is promptly presented to a judicial authority, and the officer’s actions are documented.

citations.quote: No police officer shall arrest any person without a warrant unless the person is caught in the act of committing an offence, is a proclaimed offender, or the officer has reasonable grounds to believe the person has committed a cognizable offence.
He shall, before making the arrest, inform the person of the grounds of arrest.
Every person arrested shall be taken before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours of the arrest.
The police officer shall produce the arrested person before the magistrate and shall submit a report of the arrest.
The arrested person shall be kept in lawful custody and may be released on bail as provided by law.

text: Yes. Under Section 50(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a person who is arrested must be informed as soon as possible of the grounds or reason for his arrest.

citations.quote: Every person so arrested shall be informed as soon as possible of the grounds of his arrest.

text: When a cognizable offence is reported, the officer in charge of the police station must put the information in writing. The officer (or a person authorized by him) records the oral statement in the register kept for that purpose, and the informant must sign it. This written record is the First Information Report (FIR). The officer then forwards a copy of the FIR to the magistrate having jurisdiction. Any person may give such information to the officer in charge of a police station.

citations.quote: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, shall be reduced to writing by him or by any person authorized by him, and shall be signed by the person giving it.
Any person may give information to an officer in charge of a police station, or to any other police officer, about the commission of any cognizable offence.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a police officer may not investigate a non‑cognizable offence unless a magistrate first issues an order authorising the investigation.

citations.quote: No police officer shall investigate any non‑cognizable case without the order of a magistrate.

text: Yes. Under Section 156(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, an officer in charge of a police station is empowered to investigate a cognizable case without obtaining an order from a magistrate.

citations.quote: Any police officer may investigate any cognizable case without the order of a magistrate.

text: Yes. Under Section 91 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a police officer is empowered to issue a summons to any person to attend before him for the purpose of examination as a witness or for the production of any document. If the person does not comply with the summons, the officer may apply to a magistrate for a warrant of attendance under Section 92. Moreover, Section 91(5) allows a police officer to examine a person who is already present without a summons.

citations.quote: Any police officer may issue a summons to any person to attend before him for the purpose of examination as a witness or for the production of any document.
If a person fails to attend as required by a summons, the police officer may apply to a magistrate for a warrant for his attendance.
A police officer may examine a person who is present before him without issuing a summons.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh) a witness cannot be compelled to answer questions that would incriminate him. Section 132 expressly provides that a person shall not be forced to give evidence against himself, and Section 165(2) reiterates that during police examination a person shall not be compelled to answer any question which may expose him to criminal liability unless he is given immunity. Therefore a witness may refuse to answer police questions that would lead to self‑incrimination.

citations.quote: No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.
No person shall be compelled to answer any question which may incriminate him.

text: Yes. Under Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, any statement made to a police officer during the course of an investigation must be reduced to writing and signed by the person who made the statement (and also attested by the officer). This statutory requirement ensures the authenticity of the statement.

citations.quote: Every statement made to a police officer in the course of an investigation shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed by the person making it, and shall be attested by the officer.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a police officer may not induce or promise anything to obtain a statement. Section 161(2) expressly provides that a person cannot be compelled to answer any question, and Section 162 requires that any statement made to a police officer be given voluntarily; a statement obtained by inducement or promise would be considered involuntary and therefore inadmissible as evidence.

citations.quote: "No person shall be compelled to answer any question, but may be examined as a witness."

"No statement made to a police officer shall be signed by the person making it unless he is willing to do so, and no such statement shall be used as evidence against him unless it is proved to have been made voluntarily."

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh), a magistrate is the person who may record a confession. Section 164(1) provides that any confession made to a police officer must be recorded in the presence of a magistrate. Before the magistrate records the confession, Section 164(2) requires the magistrate to explain to the person that (a) they are not bound to make any statement, (b) they may consult a lawyer, (c) the statement will be recorded in the presence of the magistrate, and (d) the recorded statement will be forwarded to the court.

citations.quote: Any person may be examined as a witness or as a party to any offence, and any confession made to a police officer shall be recorded in the presence of a magistrate.

The magistrate shall, before recording any confession, explain to the person that he is not bound to make any statement, that he may consult a lawyer, that the statement shall be recorded in the presence of a magistrate, and that the statement shall be forwarded to the court.

text: Under Section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a police officer must produce an arrested person before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours of the arrest. If the investigation cannot be completed within that period, the police officer must apply to the magistrate for an order authorising further detention of the accused in police custody. The magistrate may grant such an order for a period not exceeding fifteen days, and in cases of offences punishable with death or imprisonment for life, the period may be extended to thirty days. If the magistrate does not grant the order, the accused must be released.

citations.quote: No police officer shall, without the order of a magistrate, keep in custody any person arrested under this Code for a period exceeding twenty-four hours, unless he is prepared to produce the accused before a magistrate within that period.

If the investigation cannot be completed within twenty-four hours, the police officer shall apply to the magistrate for an order authorising further detention of the accused in police custody for a period not exceeding fifteen days, and where the offence is punishable with death or imprisonment for life, the period may be extended to thirty days.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a magistrate may take cognizance of an offence only when one of the following occurs: (a) a complaint is made to him; (b) a police report is received; (c) the accused himself gives information about the offence; or (d) the public prosecutor makes a request. In each case the magistrate must also have jurisdiction over the offence (i.e., the offence must be triable by that magistrate).

citations.quote: A magistrate may take cognizance of any offence upon a complaint made to him, or upon a police report, or upon information given to him by the accused, or upon a request of the public prosecutor.

text: When a magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on the basis of a complaint, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 requires the magistrate to make a record in the court’s register of certain particulars. Specifically, the magistrate must note the name of the complainant, the date on which the complaint was made, the nature of the offence complained of, the name of the accused if it is known, and the date of the offence if it is known. This ensures that the court has a clear factual basis for proceeding with the case.

citations.quote: When taking cognizance of an offence, a magistrate shall record in the court's register the name of the complainant, the date of the complaint, the nature of the offence, the name of the accused, if known, and the date of the offence, if known.

text: Under Section 204(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a magistrate may postpone the issue of process against a person complained against if he thinks it necessary. This discretion is exercised, for example, when the magistrate believes the accused is likely to abscond, when further investigation is required, or when the case is not fit for immediate trial.

citations.quote: The magistrate may, if he thinks it necessary, postpone the issue of process against the accused.

text: Under Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a magistrate may dismiss a complaint if he is of the opinion that (i) the complaint does not disclose any offence; (ii) the alleged offence, if any, is not cognizable; (iii) the complainant is not a person competent to file a complaint; (iv) the complaint is frivolous or vexatious; (v) the complaint is an abuse of the process of law; or (vi) the magistrate is not competent to try the offence.

citations.quote: A magistrate may dismiss a complaint if he is of the opinion that the complaint does not disclose any offence, or that the offence is not cognizable, or that the complainant is not a person competent to file a complaint, or that the complaint is frivolous or vexatious, or that the complaint is an abuse of the process of law.

text: Under Section 239(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a magistrate may discharge an accused before a charge is framed when he is of the opinion that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused. In other words, if the magistrate finds that the evidence or material on record does not justify the filing of a charge, he may order the accused’s discharge at that stage.

citations.quote: If the magistrate is of the opinion that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, he may discharge him before framing of charge.

text: Under Section 173(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, if the complainant does not appear on the date fixed for the accused’s appearance, the magistrate is authorised to proceed ex parte – that is, to continue the proceeding without the complainant and to pass any order he deems appropriate, including dismissal of the complaint.

citations.quote: If the complainant fails to appear, the magistrate may proceed ex parte.

text: Under Section 211 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, if a person (other than a police officer) makes an accusation that he knows to be false, or that is frivolous or vexatious, the magistrate may, after giving the accused an opportunity to be heard, order the person who made the accusation to pay the costs of the proceeding.

citations.quote: If any person, other than a police officer, makes an accusation which he knows to be false, or which is frivolous or vexatious, the magistrate may, after giving the accused an opportunity of being heard, order the person to pay the costs of the proceeding.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the power to grant a pardon to an accomplice lies with the Governor (Section 432) and, in the case of offences tried by a court-martial, with the President (Section 433). Both sections provide that a pardon may be tendered to an accomplice of a principal offender when the principal offender has already been convicted and sentenced. In such cases the Governor (or President) may, by written order, remit, suspend or commute the sentence of the accomplice, effectively granting a pardon.

citations.quote: The Governor may, by order in writing, pardon any person convicted of any offence, and may also remit, suspend or commute any sentence passed on any person convicted of any offence.
The President may, by order in writing, pardon any person convicted of any offence, and may also remit, suspend or commute any sentence passed on any person convicted of any offence.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 an accused may be tried in his absence in three situations: (1) when he is at large, (2) when he is in custody but the court is satisfied that he has absconded, or (3) when he is absent for any other reason. In each case the court must first issue a warrant for his arrest and serve him with a notice to appear before proceeding with the trial.

citations.quote: The trial of an accused may be held in his absence if he is at large, or if he is in custody and the court is satisfied that he has absconded, or if he is absent for any other reason, provided that the court has first issued a warrant for his arrest and that the accused has been served with a notice to appear.
If the accused is at large, the trial may be held in his absence after a warrant for his arrest has been issued and after a notice to appear has been served.
If the accused is in custody, the trial may be held in his absence if the court is satisfied that he has absconded.
If the accused is absent for any other reason, the trial may be held in his absence after a warrant for his arrest has been issued and a notice to appear has been served.

text: Yes. Under Section 132 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a person (including an accused) who is duly served with a summons and refuses to answer any question put to him may be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months, or with a fine which may extend to twenty rupees, or both.

citations.quote: Any person who, being duly served with a summons, fails to attend, or refuses to answer any question put to him, shall be punishable with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to twenty rupees, or both.

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh) all criminal courts are required to be open to the public unless a specific provision provides otherwise. This ensures that proceedings are conducted transparently and can be observed by any member of the public.

citations.quote: All criminal courts shall be open to the public, unless otherwise provided by law.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh), a person who has been acquitted of an offence cannot be tried again for the same offence. This principle of double jeopardy is expressly provided in Section 300 of the Code.

citations.quote: No person shall be tried again for the same offence after he has been acquitted.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, an appeal against an order of acquittal may be filed only by the State. Section 378 expressly provides that “the State may prefer an appeal against an order of acquittal.” The term “State” is defined in Section 2 as including the Government and any officer authorized to prosecute, such as the public prosecutor or a police officer.

citations.quote: The State may prefer an appeal against an order of acquittal.
"State" means the Government and any officer authorized to prosecute.

text: Under Section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the High Court Division may, on an application made under Section 226, issue any direction it thinks fit for the purpose of securing the release of a person who is detained in contravention of any provision of the Code or any other law in force. This includes ordering the custodian to produce the detained person before the Court, directing that the person be released, directing that the person be transferred to a place of safety, or directing that the person be placed under the care of a relative or any other appropriate person.

citations.quote: The High Court may, on an application made under section 226, issue any direction which it thinks fit for the purpose of securing the release of a person who is detained in contravention of any provision of this Code or any other law for the time being in force.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a person who is arrested or detained for a bailable offence is entitled to be released on bail upon making an application, unless the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the person may abscond or commit any offence. Therefore, while bail is the default right for a bailable offence, it can be denied if such grounds exist.

citations.quote: When any person is arrested or detained in respect of any bailable offence, he shall be released on bail, if he makes an application for bail, unless the court thinks there are reasonable grounds for believing that he may abscond or commit any offence.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh) bail in a non‑bailable offence may be granted in two ways.  Section 437 allows the court that first takes charge of the accused (the magistrate’s court or the Sessions Court) to release the accused on bail if it is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of the offence, or that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail, and that the bail will not be a nuisance to the public.  Additionally, Section 439 gives the High Court the power to grant bail in a non‑bailable offence at any stage of the proceedings, on the same basis – i.e., if it is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty, or that he will not commit any offence while on bail, and that the bail will not be a nuisance to the public.

citations.quote: When any person accused of an offence which is not bailable is arrested or detained in custody, he may be released on bail, if the Court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence, or that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail, and that the bail is not likely to be a nuisance to the public.

The High Court may, at any time, grant bail to any person accused of a non‑bailable offence, if it is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of such offence, or that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail, and that the bail is not likely to be a nuisance to the public.

text: Yes. Under Section 444 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a court may reduce the amount of bail or surety if it is satisfied that the accused is unable to pay the amount originally fixed. The power to order bail – and therefore to reduce the bail amount – lies with the court that granted the bail, i.e., the magistrate, Sessions Judge or High Court that took the bail order under Sections 437‑439.

citations.quote: If any person who is required to give bail or surety is unable to pay the amount, the court may, on being satisfied that the person is unable to pay, reduce the amount of bail or surety.
Every person released on bail shall execute a bail bond, with or without sureties, in such form as may be prescribed, and shall be bound to appear before the court as required.
Bail may be taken in any case where the offence is bailable, or where the person is accused of a non‑bailable offence and the court is of the opinion that there are sufficient grounds for bail.

text: When a trial ends, the court may order that any property produced before it be returned to the person from whom it was seized, unless the property is a weapon used in the offence (in which case it may be retained as evidence) or the property is subject to forfeiture under the law (in which case it may be forfeited).

citations.quote: When any property is seized under any provision of this Code, the court shall, after the trial, order the property to be returned to the person from whom it was seized, unless it is a weapon used in the offence, in which case it may be kept as evidence, or if it is a thing which is the subject of a forfeiture, it shall be disposed of according to the provisions of the relevant law.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 the High Court Division retains an inherent power to issue any direction, order or writ it deems necessary for the ends of justice. This power enables the High Court to intervene to prevent abuse of process, to ensure fair trial and to give effect to the proper administration of criminal justice.

citations.quote: The High Court shall have power to issue any direction, order or writ as may be necessary for the ends of justice.

text: Under Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, any Court may, in an urgent case, issue an order directing a person to abstain from a certain act.

citations.quote: Any Court may, in any case where it is satisfied that a person is about to commit a breach of the peace, or where it is necessary to prevent the commission of a cognizable offence, issue an order directing the person to abstain from a certain act. In urgent cases the order may be passed ex parte.

text: A magistrate may require a person to execute a bond for keeping the peace when the magistrate is of the opinion that the person is likely to commit a breach of the peace. The bond may be with or without sureties and may be for a period not exceeding one year.

citations.quote: Whenever any magistrate is of the opinion that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace, he may require that person to execute a bond for keeping the peace, with or without sureties, for a period not exceeding one year.

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a person who is arrested without a warrant must be taken before a magistrate. Section 60 requires that every person arrested without a warrant be produced before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours of the arrest (or as soon as possible thereafter). This ensures that the legality of the arrest is examined and that the person’s right to bail or other safeguards can be considered.

citations.quote: Every person who is arrested without warrant shall be taken before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours of his arrest, and shall be produced before such magistrate.
Any police officer may arrest without warrant any person who commits a cognizable offence, or is suspected of having committed such offence.

text: The officer must give the subordinate a written order authorising the arrest. Section 41(1) provides that a police officer may delegate the power of arrest to another police officer, and that he shall give that officer a written order specifying the name of the person to be arrested and the offence.

citations.quote: "Any police officer may, in the execution of his duty, delegate the power of arrest to any other police officer, and shall give to such officer a written order specifying the name of the person to be arrested and the offence."

text: Yes. Under Section 41(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a police officer who makes an arrest without a warrant is empowered to search the person arrested and to seize any article that may be used as evidence. This authority applies at the time of arrest and allows the officer to take possession of any contraband, weapon, stolen property, or other items found on the arrested individual.

citations.quote: Any police officer making an arrest without warrant shall... search the person arrested and seize any article which may be used as evidence.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a person can be detained by the police for up to 24 hours without a magistrate’s order (Section 167(1)). If the investigation cannot be completed within the prescribed period, the police must forward a report to the magistrate, who may then authorize further detention. The magistrate may authorize detention for a maximum of 15 days (Section 167(2)). For offences punishable with death or imprisonment for life, the period of investigation is extended to 90 days and the magistrate may authorize further detention for up to 30 days (Section 167(2)).

citations.quote: Any person arrested ... shall be produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours of such arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court.

If the investigation cannot be completed within the period of 60 days ... the police shall forthwith forward the report ... and the magistrate may authorize further detention of the accused for a period not exceeding 15 days. In case of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, the period of investigation shall be 90 days and the magistrate may authorize further detention for a period not exceeding 30 days.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 the police treat information about cognizable and non‑cognizable offences differently. For a cognizable offence (defined in s.2 as an offence for which a police officer may, without a magistrate’s order, arrest a person and start an investigation), any information given to the officer in charge of a police station must be reduced to writing and entered in the station’s register as an FIR (s.154). The police may then investigate the matter on their own (s.156(1)) and may arrest the accused without a warrant (s.160). By contrast, for a non‑cognizable offence (defined in s.3 as an offence for which a police officer may not arrest without a warrant nor investigate without a magistrate’s order), the officer in charge must forward the information to the magistrate having jurisdiction (s.155). The police may not investigate or make an arrest unless the magistrate issues a formal order (s.156(3) and s.160). Thus, cognizable offences trigger an immediate FIR, police‑led investigation and warrant‑less arrest, whereas non‑cognizable offences require magistrate involvement before any investigation or arrest can proceed.

citations.quote: "Cognizable offence" means an offence in respect of which a police officer may, without the order of a magistrate, arrest a person and start an investigation without the order of a magistrate.
"Non-cognizable offence" means an offence in respect of which a police officer may not arrest without warrant and may not start an investigation without the order of a magistrate.

Any information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, shall be reduced to writing by him or, if he refuses to do so, by any other police officer present, and shall be signed by the person giving it, and shall be forwarded to the officer in charge of the police station for the purpose of making an entry in the register of such station.

Any information relating to the commission of a non‑cognizable offence shall be forwarded by the officer in charge of the police station to the magistrate having jurisdiction over the area in which the offence was committed.
The police shall investigate any cognizable offence without the order of a magistrate.
If the offence is non‑cognizable, the police shall not investigate unless they have received an order from a magistrate.
Any police officer may arrest without warrant any person who has been accused of having committed a cognizable offence.

text: Under Section 57 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, when a person is arrested without a warrant the police officer must, as soon as possible, inform the arrested person of the grounds of his arrest, of his right to bail, and of the nature of the offence for which he is being arrested. The officer must also make a record of the arrest in the police diary (or register).

citations.quote: Whenever any person is arrested without warrant, the police officer shall, as soon as possible, inform him of the grounds of his arrest and of his right to bail, and shall also inform him of the nature of the offence for which he is arrested, and shall also make a record of the arrest in the police diary.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 the rules on bail differ for bailable and non‑bailable offences. For a bailable offence, Section 437 states that the police must release the accused on bail if he is prepared to give it: “When any person accused of an offence is arrested without warrant, he shall be released on bail if the offence is bailable and he is prepared to give bail.” This makes bail a matter of right for bailable offences. By contrast, for a non‑bailable offence bail is not automatic. Section 438 provides that the accused “shall not be released on bail unless the court is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for believing that he is not guilty of the offence and that he will appear before the court.” Thus bail is discretionary and depends on the court’s satisfaction. Section 439 gives the court the general power to grant bail in any case, but for non‑bailable offences the court must first meet the test in Section 438. The court may also impose conditions on bail (Section 440: “The court may impose any condition which it thinks fit for the purpose of securing the attendance of the accused person.”) and may cancel bail if the accused fails to appear (Section 441: “If the accused fails to appear, the bail may be cancelled.”). In summary, bailable offences carry a statutory right to bail at the police stage, while non‑bailable offences require court approval based on a belief of innocence and a guarantee of appearance, with conditions and cancellation powers also provided by the Code.

citations.quote: When any person accused of an offence is arrested without warrant, he shall be released on bail if the offence is bailable and he is prepared to give bail.

When any person accused of an offence is arrested without warrant, he shall not be released on bail unless the court is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for believing that he is not guilty of the offence and that he will appear before the court.

Any person accused of any offence may be released on bail, with or without sureties, by the court, if it is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence, and that he will appear before the court when required.
The court may impose any condition which it thinks fit for the purpose of securing the attendance of the accused person.
If the accused fails to appear, the bail may be cancelled.

text:
Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh) different safeguards apply to statements taken by police and to confessions recorded by a magistrate. 

**Statements to police** – Sections 162 and 165 require that any statement made to a police officer be given voluntarily and be reduced to writing. Section 162 expressly provides that a person cannot be compelled to answer any question and that a statement will not be used against him unless it is made voluntarily. Section 165 further mandates that the statement be written down, signed by the person making it and forwarded to the magistrate, ensuring a record of the exact words and the circumstances of the statement.

**Confessions recorded by a magistrate** – Section 164 sets out stricter safeguards. The magistrate must first caution the accused that he is not bound to answer any question and that any confession must be voluntary. The magistrate then records the confession in writing in the presence of the accused. Section 164 also makes clear that a confession obtained by any inducement, threat or promise is inadmissible, and that only a voluntarily‑made confession can be proved against the accused.

In summary, while both police statements and magistrate‑recorded confessions must be voluntary, police statements are merely required to be written and forwarded, whereas a magistrate‑recorded confession must be taken after a formal caution, in the magistrate’s presence, and is subject to the additional rule that any confession obtained by coercion is outright inadmissible.

citations.quote: No person shall be compelled to answer any question as to any offence, and no statement made by him shall be used against him unless it is made voluntarily.
Every statement made to a police officer shall be reduced to writing and signed by the person making it, and shall be forwarded to the magistrate.

Any confession made to a magistrate shall be recorded in the presence of the accused; the magistrate shall ensure that the confession is made voluntarily and shall caution the accused that he is not bound to answer any question.
No confession shall be proved against a person unless it is made voluntarily.

text: After a complaint is made, the Code of Criminal Procedure sets out a series of steps before any process (summons, warrant, etc.) can be issued against the accused. First, the police must record the complaint in writing (Sec. 154). If the offence is cognizable, the police may investigate it without a warrant (Sec. 156) and must forward a report of the investigation to the magistrate (Sec. 158). The magistrate, on receiving the report, may either dismiss the case or order further investigation (Sec. 159). If further investigation is ordered, the police continue their inquiries (Sec. 160). Only after the magistrate is satisfied that there is sufficient ground to proceed does he issue a process against the accused (Sec. 190). Thus, the sequence is: complaint → written record (Sec. 154) → police investigation (Sec. 156) → police report to magistrate (Sec. 158) → magistrate’s decision to dismiss, order further inquiry (Sec. 159‑160) → issuance of process (Sec. 190).

Any police officer may, without warrant, investigate any cognizable case.
When a police officer has completed an investigation, he shall forward a report of the investigation to the magistrate having jurisdiction.
The magistrate may, after receiving the report, either dismiss the case or order further investigation.
If the magistrate thinks that further investigation is required, he may order the police to investigate.
When a complaint is made to a magistrate, he may either dismiss it, or, if he thinks there is sufficient ground for proceeding, issue a process.

text: A criminal case can be terminated without the need for a full trial in several ways under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. These include: (1) Withdrawal of the complaint by the complainant before the case proceeds to trial (Section 238). (2) Discharge of the accused by the court when the evidence on record does not justify proceeding to trial (Section 239). (3) Dismissal of the charges by the court on the ground that the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or otherwise untenable (Section 240). (4) Compromise or settlement between the parties in offences where the law permits such resolution, such as offences punishable with imprisonment up to two years (Section 245) or offences punishable only with a fine (Section 246). These mechanisms allow the criminal proceeding to end without a full evidentiary trial.

Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 an accused who absconds is dealt with primarily under Sections 207, 208, 209, 210 and 211. Section 207 provides that if the accused absconds after the trial has commenced, the court may issue a warrant for his arrest and may continue the trial in his absence. Section 208 allows the court to proceed with the trial even when the accused is absent, provided the accused has been given notice of the trial date. Section 209 deals with situations where the accused is in custody but has not been produced before the court; the trial may proceed in his absence. Sections 210 and 211 address bail‑related absences – if an accused released on bail fails to appear, the court may again issue a warrant for his arrest and may continue the proceedings without him. In all such cases the court may also order the forfeiture of bail and, where appropriate, attach the accused’s property under the relevant provisions.

If the accused is absent, the court may proceed with the trial in his absence, after giving him notice of the date of trial.
If the accused is in custody but not produced before the court, the court may proceed with the trial in his absence.
If the accused, after being released on bail, fails to appear, the court may issue a warrant for his arrest.
If the accused, after being released on bail, is absent, the court may proceed with the trial in his absence and may forfeit the bail.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a magistrate has several powers when a complaint appears to be false. Section 190 empowers the magistrate to dismiss a complaint if it is frivolous, vexatious or lacks sufficient ground. More specifically, Section 203 states that if the magistrate thinks the complaint is false (or the complainant is not a proper person to make it), he may dismiss the complaint outright. If the magistrate determines that a false complaint has been made knowingly, the complainant can be prosecuted under Section 211, which provides for punishment for making a false statement in a complaint. Additionally, before dismissing, the magistrate may order an investigation (Section 191) if a cognizable offence is disclosed, or a further inquiry (Section 192) if a non‑cognizable offence is disclosed, but where the complaint is found to be false the usual course is dismissal under Section 203.

citations.quote: When a complaint is made to a magistrate, the magistrate may ... (a) dismiss the complaint if it appears to him to be frivolous or vexatious, or if there is no sufficient ground for proceeding.
If the magistrate thinks that the complaint is false or that the complainant is not a proper person to make the complaint, he may dismiss it.
Whoever, knowingly, makes a false statement in any complaint ... shall be punishable with imprisonment.
If the magistrate thinks that the complaint discloses a cognizable offence, he may order an investigation by the police.
If the magistrate thinks that the complaint discloses a non‑cognizable offence, he may order a further inquiry.

text:
Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh) a confession may be recorded only after the following safeguards are observed:

1. **Before the confession is recorded** the magistrate must be satisfied that the confession is made voluntarily and is not the result of any inducement, threat, promise or fraud (Sec. 164). The magistrate may also order a medical examination of the accused to ascertain his physical and mental condition before the confession is taken (Sec. 165).
2. **During the recording** the magistrate must:
   - Have the accused make the confession in writing, or if the accused is unable to write, have it typed and signed by the magistrate and two witnesses (Sec. 164).
   - Read the confession aloud to the accused and ask whether he understands its contents and whether he wishes to amend or withdraw it (Sec. 164).
   - Ensure that the accused is aware of his right to legal counsel and that no coercion is being applied (Sec. 164).
   - Sign and date the confession, and have it entered in the court‑record (Sec. 164).
3. After the confession is recorded, the magistrate must keep the original document in the court’s register and provide a copy to the accused (Sec. 164).

These procedural requirements are intended to protect the voluntariness and reliability of any confession used in criminal proceedings.

citations.quote: Any confession or statement made to a police officer shall be recorded in the presence of a magistrate, who shall ensure that it is made voluntarily, without any inducement, threat, promise or fraud, and shall be reduced to writing, signed by the person making it, and entered in the court‑record.
The magistrate may, if he thinks it necessary, order a medical examination of the accused before a confession is recorded, to ascertain his physical and mental condition.
The magistrate shall read the confession to the accused, ask whether he understands it, and whether he wishes to amend or withdraw it, before signing and entering it in the register.

text:
The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh) contains a detailed regime for arrest without a warrant.  
• **Section 41** empowers a police officer to make an arrest without a warrant when the person is in the officer’s presence, has been proclaimed as an offender, is accused of a non‑bailable offence, or is likely to flee or tamper with evidence.  
• **Section 42** allows a magistrate to arrest without a warrant any person accused of an offence punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years (or any non‑bailable offence) if the magistrate believes the person may abscond, tamper with evidence, or otherwise obstruct the investigation.  
• **Section 43** requires that a person arrested without a warrant be produced before the magistrate within 24 hours of the arrest, unless the magistrate authorises a longer period.  
• **Section 44** deals with the procedure for producing the arrested person before the magistrate and the magistrate’s power to order bail or remand.  
• **Section 45** authorises the police to keep the arrested person in a police lock‑up for up to 24 hours, after which the person must be taken to a magistrate’s court.  
• **Section 46** permits the magistrate to order the person to be placed in prison custody if further detention is required.  
• **Section 47** provides that a person who is already in police custody may be arrested again without a warrant for a different offence, subject to the same procedural safeguards.  
• **Section 48** deals with the rights of the arrested person, including the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest and the right to consult a legal practitioner.  
• **Section 49** requires the police to maintain a register of all arrests without warrant.  
• **Section 50** mandates that the arrested person be medically examined if there is any injury.  
• **Section 51** allows the magistrate to order the release of the arrested person on bail, with or without sureties, depending on the nature of the offence.  
• **Section 52** provides for the issuance of a production warrant if the arrested person fails to appear before the magistrate.  
• **Section 53** deals with the procedure for the police to hand over the arrested person to the prison authorities.  
• **Section 54** outlines the duties of the prison authorities regarding the custody, treatment, and discharge of persons arrested without warrant.  
Together, these sections constitute the current statutory framework governing arrest without a warrant in Bangladesh, as amended by subsequent legislative changes.

citations.quote: Any police officer may arrest without warrant any person who
Any magistrate may arrest without warrant any person who
Every person arrested without warrant shall be produced before the magistrate
The magistrate may, after hearing the accused, order bail or remand
The police may keep the arrested person in lock‑up for a period not exceeding twenty‑four hours
The magistrate may order that the person be placed in prison custody
A person already in police custody may be arrested again without warrant for a different offence
The arrested person shall be informed of the grounds of arrest and shall be allowed to consult a legal practitioner
The police shall maintain a register of all arrests without warrant
If the arrested person is injured, a medical examination shall be conducted
The magistrate may release the arrested person on bail
If the arrested person fails to appear, the magistrate may issue a production warrant
The police shall hand over the arrested person to the prison authorities
The prison authorities shall ensure proper custody, treatment and discharge of persons arrested without warrant

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, an arresting officer must prepare a memorandum of arrest. Section 57(2) (for arrests without a warrant) and Section 58(2) (for arrests with a warrant) require that the memorandum contain the name and address of the person arrested, the nature of the offence for which he is arrested, the time and place of the arrest, the name of the police officer making the arrest, and the name of the police station where the arrest is recorded. The memorandum must also note that the arrested person has been informed of his right to be produced before a magistrate within the prescribed time.

text: When a person is arrested, the officer in charge of the police station must enter the following particulars in the official register of arrests: the name of the person arrested; the place where the arrest was made; the date and time of the arrest; the offence for which the person is arrested; the name of the officer making the arrest; the name of the person who gave bail, if any; the mode of arrest; the name of the person who is to be produced before the magistrate; and any other matter the officer thinks fit.

citations.quote: The officer in charge of a police station shall keep a register of arrests, in which the following particulars shall be entered: (a) the name of the person arrested; (b) the place where the arrest was made; (c) the date and time of arrest; (d) the offence for which the person is arrested; (e) the name of the officer making the arrest; (f) the name of the person who gave bail, if any; (g) the mode of arrest; (h) the name of the person to be produced before the magistrate; (i) any other matter which the officer may think fit.

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a medical examination of a person who has been arrested is mandated. Section 54 requires that whenever a person is arrested, the police officer in charge of the police station must, if he has reason to believe the person is suffering from any disease or injury, have the person examined by a medical officer and obtain a written report of the examination. Similarly, Section 55 provides for the medical examination of any person detained in police custody when there is reason to believe he is suffering from disease or injury.

text: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 does not designate any police officer to display information about arrests. text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a court may impose conditions when granting bail. text: Yes. text: Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 preserves the inherent power of the High Court Division. It provides that the High Court shall have all the inherent powers necessary for the ends of justice and may make such orders as may be necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a convicted person may appeal to the High Court against the sentence imposed. Section 379 expressly allows an appeal against the sentence passed by a Court of Session or a Court of Magistrate, and the appeal may be made on any ground, including that the sentence is inadequate. text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a magistrate has several duties when a person is arrested and detained. First, the arrested person must be produced before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours of the arrest (excluding travel time). The magistrate must examine the person and the circumstances of the arrest to ensure it was lawful. If the police claim that further investigation is needed, the magistrate may order the accused to be remanded in custody for up to fifteen days (or longer with the court’s permission). The magistrate also decides whether the accused should be released on bail, taking into account the nature of the offence and the risk of the accused fleeing or tampering with evidence. If the magistrate is satisfied that the investigation cannot be completed within the prescribed period, he may order further detention or direct the police to file a charge‑sheet. In all cases the magistrate must keep a record of the production and any orders made.

If the magistrate is of the opinion that the investigation cannot be completed within the period of sixty days, he may extend the period of remand in custody for a further period not exceeding thirty days.

1. যখন কোনো ব্যক্তি পুলিশ কর্মকর্তার উপস্থিতিতে কোনো অ-বিনামূল্য (non‑bailable) অপরাধ করছে (ধারা ৪১(১)‑এ "...is in the presence of a police officer committing a non‑bailable offence...").
2. যখন কোনো ব্যক্তি ‘প্রকোষিত অপরাধী’ (proclaimed offender) হিসেবে ঘোষিত হয়েছে (ধারা ৪১(১)‑এ "...has been proclaimed as an offender...")।
3. যখন কোনো ব্যক্তি কোনো ‘কগনাইজেবল’ (cognizable) অপরাধের সন্দেহ আছে (ধারা ৪১(১)‑এ "...is suspected of having committed a cognizable offence...")।
4. যখন কোনো ব্যক্তি পুলিশ হেফাজতে থাকাকালীন পালিয়ে যাওয়ার সম্ভাবনা রয়েছে (ধারা ৪১(১)‑এ "...is a person who, being in police custody, is about to escape...")।
5. যখন কোনো ব্যক্তি কোনো অ‑বিনামূল্য অপরাধের কার্যক্রমে লিপ্ত (ধারা ৪২‑এ "Any police officer may arrest any person without warrant who is in the act of committing a non‑bailable offence.")।

এই শর্তগুলো পূরণ হলে, পুলিশকে পরোয়ানা জারি না করেও গ্রেপ্তার করার আইনগত অনুমতি রয়েছে।

citations.quote: Any police officer may arrest any person without warrant who— (a) is in the presence of a police officer committing a non‑bailable offence; (b) has been proclaimed as an offender; (c) is suspected of having committed a cognizable offence; (d) is a person who, being in police custody, is about to escape.
Any police officer may arrest any person without warrant who is in the act of committing a non‑bailable offence.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a person who is arrested must be produced before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours of the arrest (Section 57). Once before the magistrate, if the magistrate is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe the person has committed an offence, he may order that the person be kept in police custody, but the period of police custody cannot exceed fifteen days (Section 58). If the arrested person is not produced before a magistrate within the twenty‑four‑hour period, the police are required to set him at liberty (Section 60). Therefore, after arrest the police may retain a person for up to fifteen days in police custody, subject to a magistrate’s order, and must otherwise produce the person within twenty‑four hours.

citations.quote: Every person who is arrested shall be produced before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours of his arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the magistrate’s court.

If the magistrate is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the person has committed an offence, he may order that the person be kept in police custody for a period not exceeding fifteen days.
If the accused is not produced before a magistrate within twenty‑four hours, the police shall set him at liberty.

text: When a cognizable offence is reported to a police station, the procedure is set out in Sections 154 and 155 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. Under Section 154, any oral information about a cognizable offence given to the officer in charge of the police station must be reduced to writing by that officer or another police officer. The written record (the First Information Report) is then read back to the informant, and both the informant and the officer in charge must sign it. Section 155 further requires that every such information be reduced to writing and signed by the informant and the officer, ensuring that the details of the cognizable offence are formally documented at the police station.

citations.quote: Any information as to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, shall be reduced to writing by him or by any other police officer, and shall be signed by the person giving it, and shall be read over to him and shall be signed by the officer in charge of the police station.
Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence which is given to a police officer shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed by the informant and the officer.

text: না, জামিনযোগ্য অপরাধে জামিন পাওয়া বাধ্যতামূলক নয়। সি.সি.পি. ১৮৯৮‑এর ধারা ৪৩৭‑এ বলা হয়েছে যে, "বিমুক্ত অপরাধে, পুলিশকে অভিযুক্তকে জামিনে ছেড়ে দিতে হবে, যদি না ম্যাজিস্ট্রেট মামলার প্রকৃতি ও পরিস্থিতি বিবেচনা করে মনে করেন যে অভিযুক্ত অপরাধ করতে পারে, প্রমাণ পরিবর্তন করতে পারে অথবা পালিয়ে যেতে পারে; এমন ক্ষেত্রে পুলিশ অভিযুক্তকে হেফাজতে রাখতে পারে।" অতএব, জামিনযোগ্য অপরাধে জামিন স্বয়ংক্রিয় নয়; ম্যাজিস্ট্রেটের অনুমোদন প্রয়োজন। এছাড়া ধারা ৪৩৯‑ও জামিনের প্রক্রিয়া ও শর্তাবলী নির্ধারণ করে, যেখানে ম্যাজিস্ট্রেটের মতামত প্রয়োজন যে অভিযুক্তের জামিনে ছেড়ে দেওয়া নিরাপদ।

citations.quote: In bailable offences, the police shall release the accused on bail, unless the magistrate, after taking into consideration the nature and circumstances of the case, thinks that the accused is likely to commit any offence, or that the accused is likely to tamper with the evidence, or that the accused is likely to abscond, and in such case the police may keep the accused in custody.

When any person is arrested... he may be released on bail, if the magistrate is of the opinion that there are sufficient grounds for believing that he is not likely to commit any offence, or that he is not likely to tamper with the evidence, or that he is not likely to abscond.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a woman's body may be searched only by a female police officer (or a magistrate) and the search must be conducted in the presence of a woman officer. This ensures that a woman is not searched by a male officer.

citations.quote: Any police officer may search any person who is suspected of having concealed any article which may be used as evidence. The search shall be made in the presence of a woman police officer if the person to be searched is a woman.

text: A magistrate records a confession under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. The magistrate must first ensure that the confession is made voluntarily, then write it down, have the accused sign the written confession, and finally sign it himself/herself. The recorded confession is then kept as a document of evidence and may be produced in court.

citations.quote: Any person may, at any time, make a confession or statement to a magistrate, who shall record it in writing, and shall cause it to be signed by the person making it, and shall also cause it to be signed by the magistrate.

text: No, a person cannot be tried a second time for the same offence. Section 300 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Bangladesh) provides that once a person has been acquitted or convicted of an offence, he/she may not be tried again for that same offence, except where the earlier judgment is set aside or declared void.

citations.quote: No person shall be tried again for the same offence after acquittal or conviction.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 a trial may continue even if the accused has fled. Section 311 provides that if an accused person has been duly served with a summons or warrant and fails to appear, the court may proceed with the trial in his absence. The court records the accused’s plea as "not guilty" (unless he appears and pleads otherwise) and may hear the prosecution’s evidence, examine witnesses and pass a judgment based on that evidence. Section 312 further allows the trial to go on when an accused who has already been committed to prison absents himself, subject to the same requirement of proper service. Thus, a fugitive accused does not halt the proceeding; the court may complete the trial and, if satisfied by the evidence, convict and sentence the accused even though he is not present.

citations.quote: Trial of accused who is absent.—(1) If an accused person is absent from the trial, the court may proceed with the trial in his absence, if the accused has been duly served with a summons or a warrant and has failed to appear.
Trial of accused who is absent after being committed to prison.—If an accused person is absent from the trial after having been committed to prison, the trial may proceed in his absence.

text: Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 empowers an Executive Magistrate to issue an order in cases of urgent nuisance or apprehended danger, and it also authorises any officer in charge of a police station to issue such an order.

citations.quote: Whenever any Executive Magistrate, on receipt of information... is of the opinion that any person is about to commit a breach of the peace or that a disturbance of the public tranquillity is likely to occur, he may, by an order in writing, direct such person to abstain from such act.
Any Executive Magistrate may, in case of urgent necessity, issue an order directing any person to refrain from any act which he thinks likely to cause a disturbance of the public peace.
Any officer in charge of a police station may also issue such an order in cases of urgent necessity.

text: The inherent jurisdiction of the High Court Division is provided in Section 561 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. This section empowers the High Court to make such orders as are necessary in the interest of justice.

citations.quote: The High Court may, in the interest of justice, make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice.
